Julio Cortázar. Born in nineteen fourteen and dying in nineteen eighty-four, Cortázar was an Argentine writer and innovator of the Latin American literary boom, renowned for his experimental narrative forms and philosophical depth.

Born in Belgium but raised in Argentina, he lived much of his adult life in Paris, a diaspora writer inhabiting multiple cultures. His masterpiece Hopscotch, published in nineteen sixty-three, is a novel that invites the reader to navigate its chapters in multiple orders, challenging the Western page-bound, linear novel form.

Cortázar was a master of the short story. Works like The House Taken Over and Instructions on How to Climb a Staircase are brilliant miniatures of the fantastic invading the ordinary. His narrative experiments reflect influence from existentialism, jazz, which he loved passionately, and a philosophical playfulness about language, consciousness, and reality.

He was part of the nineteen-sixties boom generation alongside García Márquez, Vargas Llosa, and Carlos Fuentes, though his work was more formally experimental and less committed to social realism than theirs. Gregory Rabassa's translation of Hopscotch into English in nineteen sixty-six is the definitive English version and made Cortázar's work accessible to English readers; translation was crucial to his global influence.

In his later years, Cortázar became politically engaged, supporting the Cuban Revolution and other leftist causes, though his earlier work was not explicitly political.
